newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech govt agrees on 50 percent average rent hike.
newsitem.headline: Czech govt agrees on 50 percent average rent hike.

text.p: The Czech government agreed on Thursday to raise state-controlleed rents by an average of 50 percent from July 1, the CTK news agency said.

It quoted Labour & Social Affairs Minister Jindrich Vodicka as saying after a late-night government meeting that the rent increase would be partially covered by compensation payments for low income and needy families.
The were no details of the degree of compesnation.
The government also agreed to make available interest-free, 10-year loans of 200,000 crowns to help people buy new houses.

CTK said the loans and other social subsidies would amount to four billion crowns, and that the funds would come from the budget and the National Property Fund (NPF). It did not give a detailed break-down of the source of funds.

Earlier in the marathon session, the government approved a plan to raise the value added tax on electricity and natural gas to 22 percent from five percent, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus told a news conference.
The hike in the energy VAT, which must still be approved by parliament, would begin on January 1, 1998, Klaus said.
A global agreement on raising rents had been reached, but details were still to be worked out, he said.
However, the cabinet agreed on Wednesday to delay discussion of any changes to income and excise taxes.

Economists have said the price deregulation moves could add several percentage points to the inflation rate but also suppress high levels of domestic demand, which are conbtributing to a widening trade gap.
Czech consumer prices rose 0.3 percent in February for a year-on-year rise of 7.3 percent, compared with an 8.8 average rise in 1996.
Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik said on February 28 that price deregulation in the housing and energy sector could push inflation up to 9.5 percent by the end of this year.

Many Czechs still live in flats with artificially low rents and with energy bills subsidised by industrial users. This has made deregulation one of the stickiest political issues in the Czech Republic.
